title: Mechanistic insights into consumption of the food additive xanthan gum by the human gut microbiota
authors: Ostrowski MP, La Rosa SL, Kunath BJ, Robertson A, Pereira G, Hagen LH, et al.
population: Faecal enrichment cultures from 80 and then 60 adults, bacterial isolates, recombinant enzymes, published human and environmental metagenomes, and germ-free mice colonised with a human microbiota

result: In an initial survey of faecal cultures from 80 adults under gentamicin selection, one culture degraded xanthan gum; in a second survey of 60 adults without antibiotic, about half of the cultures grew on xanthan gum and lost its viscosity. Across 20 degrading communities passaged ten times, the only operational taxonomic unit present above 0.5% in all of them was an uncultured Ruminococcaceae genus, R.UCG13, whose locus was conserved at above 95% amino acid identity. A secreted R.UCG13 glycoside hydrolase family 5 enzyme, RuGH5a, cleaves the xanthan backbone at the reducing end of the unbranched glucose, yielding pentasaccharide repeating units, and requires its three additional domains for activity; cell-free culture supernatant released pentameric and decameric oligosaccharides, while the intracellular fraction was needed for further saccharification; it hydrolyses native and lyase-treated xanthan with comparable specificity, unlike earlier xanthanases that prefer lyase-treated substrate by 600-fold or more. A polysaccharide lyase family 8 enzyme acted on the oligosaccharides but not on the polymer, removing the terminal pyruvylated mannose; a GH88 removed the resulting unsaturated glucuronic acid, two GH38 enzymes hydrolysed the trisaccharide, two carbohydrate esterases removed acetyl groups and a GH94 phosphorylase cleaved cellobiose, completing saccharification. Bacteroides intestinalis isolated from the same culture grew on the oligosaccharides but not on polymeric xanthan gum, and every gene of its polysaccharide utilisation locus rose more than 100-fold on the oligosaccharides compared with glucose. The R.UCG13 locus was detected in faecal metagenomes of all industrialised populations sampled and in none of the Yanomami, Hadza or Burkina Faso datasets, whose small size leaves false negatives possible; an expanded search of 21,762 metagenomes, 102,860 genome bins and 72,491 isolate genomes returned 35 hits for the locus, all in human microbiome datasets, including senior adults, children and a 12-month-old infant; the B. intestinalis locus was absent from the Japanese and Danish or Spanish datasets. In germ-free mice colonised with a human microbiota containing R.UCG13, its expansion depended on dietary xanthan gum, and a gavaged oligosaccharide-consuming B. intestinalis strain displaced the endogenous strain in the xanthan gum group. A xanthan utilisation locus with similar architecture was found in mouse faecal metagenomes.
